title: Storm control and the circuit breaker

story: Tuesday, 10:02. You know this morning already: a merged PR broke a test in the projects table, main went red, and one CI fixer is gathering every red build of that one problem. The fingerprint is doing its job. Then, at 10:14, a new image for our GitHub runners rolls out, and it cannot reach the package mirror. Every install step starts to fail: npm ci in frontend CI, uv sync in cloud and client CI. Each job dies on a different package, so each red build has a different first error line, and by 10:26 seven new fingerprints have arrived.

Seven fingerprints means seven fixer runs. Each one would claim a VM, run the failed commands, find them green in the VM, because the VM's network is fine, and post its own hand-off to the alerts channel. That is seven machines and seven messages for one broken runner image, which no agent can fix anyway. What the morning needs is not seven agents. It needs one person, paged once.
hook.question: How does the platform notice that red builds have stopped being a code problem, and stop every fixer at once?

p: The last lesson gave every problem a name: one fingerprint, one fixer run. That makes counting easy. Ten red builds of one broken test are still one run, so the number of fixer runs that started recently is the number of new root causes. On a normal day that number is one, sometimes two. Real code breaks one thing at a time, because each merge is one change. When many new causes appear at once, across frontend, cloud and client, the common cause is almost always the environment: the runners, the package mirror, the QA environment. Agents cannot fix any of those, so the rule is simple. More than 5 new fingerprints in 15 minutes switches on incident mode.

The count comes from Temporal itself, with no extra database. Temporal keeps a searchable list of every run, called visibility, and you can ask it questions in a small SQL-like language. Each routine run carries search attributes, which are indexed fields we set ourselves: Routine says which routine it is, and RunKind says what kind of work, such as cifix for a red-main fixer. So "how many fixer runs started in the last 15 minutes?" is one query and one call.

notes.text: A 15-minute window, and at most 5 new causes in it.
Only the routines that fix red CI. Upgrade and bug fixers are not part of a red-main storm.
The visibility query: fixer runs of these routines started after since.
One fixer run is one fingerprint, so this counts new root causes.
setIfAbsent returns true only for the caller that set the flag. Everyone after it finds the flag already there.
So the on-call person is paged once per incident, not once per run.

p: Incident mode is one flag, routines:fixers:paused, in the same flag store that the kill switch uses. Setting it does three things. The on-call person gets one page, through PagerDuty. The alerts channel, #ai-agents-alerts, gets one post with each fingerprint's first error line and a Resume fixers button. And every new fixer run parks at its gate: the pre-run gate sees incident mode, waits on a Temporal timer, and never claims a VM. A parked run costs nothing, because a sleeping workflow holds no machine.

The trick that makes the page come only once is setIfAbsent: set the flag only if nobody has set it yet, and tell me whether I was the one who set it. Seven runs may ask the question within a minute. The first one sets the flag and pages, and the other six see the flag already set and stay quiet. You will build exactly this in the lab with a file that is created only if it does not exist.

At 10:40 a person rolls the runner image back and presses Resume fixers. The parked runs wake up and first check that main is still red at its latest commit. For the seven install failures it is green now, so each ends as not_needed, with nothing to do. The run for the broken test from 10:02 is a real code problem, so it is still red, and it carries on to its VM. The storm costs one page and zero VMs, and the real problem still gets its fixer.

deeper.h: Go deeper: testing the storm before it happens
p: Nobody wants to discover in a real storm that the rule is wrong. The plan tests it with a replay: in a test namespace, eight saved red-build events are sent within two minutes, and the test passes only if there is exactly one page and zero acquireSandbox calls. Fakes stand in for PagerDuty and Slack, and the visibility count is the real one from a Temporal test server.

read.h: A smaller breaker for one routine
p: Storm control watches all fixers together. One routine can also go wrong on its own: a new skill confuses it, and its runs start to fail or be rejected one after another. The answer has the same shape, in a smaller size. It is called a circuit breaker, after the switch in a house that cuts the power when too much current flows and stays off until someone resets it. After every run, the routine's last 5 finished runs are checked. If 3 of them failed or were rejected, the breaker trips: the routine is paused with routine:<name>:paused, and its owner gets a message with the 5 runs and their reasons, and a Resume button.

What counts matters. When a run ends, routineRun sets the search attribute RoutineOutcome: merged, closed, rejected (a scope-judge veto, a false heal, or a PR a person closed), failed (no fix found), handed_off or not_needed. Only failed and rejected count against the routine. handed_off usually means the environment was the problem, and not_needed means main healed by itself, and neither is the routine's fault. Without that line, a routine would be paused for the runner image's mistakes too.

notes.text: Only these two outcomes are the routine's own fault.
A Temporal visibility list of this routine's finished runs, newest first.
Fewer than 5 runs, or fewer than 3 bad: no trip.
The same pause flag the merge-rate rule uses, so the gate needs to read only one flag per routine.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why there is no third breaker for ping-pong
p: Ping-pong is two fixes undoing each other: one fixer's change breaks something, the next fixer reverts part of it, and the original failure comes back. The fingerprint already catches this. A fingerprint that returns after its run closed means main was never green in between, and the REJECT_DUPLICATE reuse policy from the last lesson refuses the start and sends the problem to a person. So the platform needs no extra rule for it.

lab.title: A storm on your laptop
needs: Node 22.18 or newer (it runs .ts files directly)
lab.goal: Start a storm of fixer runs on a local Temporal server, count new fingerprints with a visibility query, and write a storm check that pages only once.

guess.q: Between 10:14 and 10:26, seven new fingerprints arrive, and each new run calls stormCheck. With setIfAbsent, how many pages does the on-call person get?

options.text: Seven, one for each new fingerprint.
options.why: That would be a page per run, which is the noise this lesson removes.

options.text: Two: the sixth run crosses the limit and pages, and the seventh pages again.
options.why: The seventh run finds the flag already set, so setIfAbsent returns false and it stays quiet.

options.text: One: the first run that sees more than 5 sets the flag and pages, and later runs find the flag set.
options.why: setIfAbsent lets exactly one caller win. The page goes out once per incident.

follow.say: Start a local Temporal server that knows our two search attributes, Routine and RunKind. Leave this terminal open.
follow.see:
Temporal CLI 1.9.1 (Server 1.32.0, UI 2.54.1)

Temporal Server:      localhost:7233
Temporal Persistence: in-memory
Temporal UI:          http://localhost:8233

follow.say: In a second terminal, start the 10:02 fixer run for the broken test. There is no worker, so the run just stays open, which is all we need for counting.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g5-4 && cd ~/academy-labs/g5-4
temporal workflow start --type routineRun --task-queue ai-agents-cifix --workflow-id cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4 \
  --search-attribute 'Routine="fe-ci-fixer"' --search-attribute 'RunKind="cifix"'
follow.see:
Running execution:
  WorkflowId  cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4
  RunId       01a142b4-97d8-7196-8b9b-48c9e3cce18b
  Type        routineRun
  Namespace   default
  TaskQueue   ai-agents-cifix

follow.say: Ask Temporal how many fixer runs started in the last 15 minutes. This is the question stormCheck asks.
follow.do:
SINCE=$(node -e 'console.log(new Date(Date.now() - 15 * 60_000).toISOString())')
temporal workflow count --query "WorkflowType='routineRun' AND RunKind='cifix' AND StartTime > '$SINCE'"

follow.say: Now the runner image breaks: seven new fingerprints from frontend and backend CI, each with its own fixer run.
follow.do:
for run in fe-ci-fixer:9c1e04b2a7f3 fe-ci-fixer:52d8e1a0c4b9 be-ci-fixer:e07a3b9d2c15 be-ci-fixer:4b6f0d81e2a7 \
           be-ci-fixer:b2c9a7e40f13 fe-ci-fixer:71a0f3c8d9e2 be-ci-fixer:0d4e8b2f6a91; do
  temporal workflow start --type routineRun --task-queue ai-agents-cifix --workflow-id "cifix:fcp:${run#*:}" \
    --search-attribute "Routine=\"${run%%:*}\"" --search-attribute 'RunKind="cifix"' > /dev/null
  echo "started cifix:fcp:${run#*:}  (${run%%:*})"
done
follow.see:
started cifix:fcp:9c1e04b2a7f3  (fe-ci-fixer)
started cifix:fcp:52d8e1a0c4b9  (fe-ci-fixer)
started cifix:fcp:e07a3b9d2c15  (be-ci-fixer)
…
started cifix:fcp:0d4e8b2f6a91  (be-ci-fixer)

follow.say: Count again. One cause an hour is normal; eight in a few minutes is a storm.
follow.do:
SINCE=$(node -e 'console.log(new Date(Date.now() - 15 * 60_000).toISOString())')
temporal workflow count --query "WorkflowType='routineRun' AND RunKind='cifix' AND StartTime > '$SINCE'"

follow.say: Install the Temporal client and write the flag store. A file created with the wx flag fails if it already exists, which is exactly setIfAbsent.
follow.see:
added 43 packages, and audited 44 packages in 4s
found 0 vulnerabilities

lab.build: Write storm.ts. It connects to Temporal (use process.env.TEMPORAL_ADDRESS ?? "localhost:7233"), counts routineRun runs with RunKind 'cifix' that started in the last 15 minutes with client.workflow.count(query), and prints normal when the count is 5 or less. Above 5 it calls setIfAbsent("routines-fixers-paused", reason): if that returns true it prints that the fixers are paused and the on-call person is paged once; if false it prints that the fixers were already paused and no second page goes out. Run it twice, then delete the flags folder (that is pressing Resume fixers) and run it once more.
checks: The first node storm.ts prints incident: fixers paused, paging on-call once: 8 new failure fingerprints in 15 minutes.
The second run prints incident: already paused, no second page.
After rm -rf flags, the next run pages again, because a new incident starts.
If you change WINDOW_MS to one minute and wait two minutes, storm.ts prints normal: 0 new fingerprints in 15 minutes (the message still says 15; the window is what changed).
You stopped the dev server with Ctrl+C at the end, which also deletes every run, because it keeps them in memory.
lab.fix: A teammate found setIfAbsent "too clever". Setting a flag twice is harmless, they said, so they changed flags.ts to always write the file and always return true. Make the same change and run node storm.ts three times: the on-call person is paged three times for one broken runner image, and in a real storm every new fixer run would page again. Explain why setting the flag twice is harmless but paging twice is not, and put setIfAbsent back.
explain: Why does counting fixer runs count root causes, and not red builds?
Why are many new fingerprints at once a sign of the environment rather than the code?
In the circuit breaker, why do handed_off and not_needed not count against a routine?
lab.done: Your storm check counts eight fingerprints, pages once, stays quiet the second time, and pages again after the flag is cleared.

check.q: Why does stormCheck count fixer runs instead of red CI builds?

options.text: Because red builds are not stored anywhere the orchestrator can read
options.why: GitHub keeps every run. The reason is what the count means, not where the data is.

options.text: Because each fixer run is one fingerprint, so the count is the number of new root causes
options.why: Ten red builds of one broken test are one run. Many runs in a short time means many causes at once, which points to the environment.

options.text: Because counting runs is cheaper than counting builds
options.why: Both are one query. Counting builds would answer a different, less useful question.

check.q: Incident mode is on. A new fingerprint arrives and its fixer run reaches the gate. What does it do?

options.text: It claims a VM but waits inside it until the incident is over
options.why: A VM that waits costs money. The point of parking at the gate is that no machine is claimed.

options.text: It pages the on-call person again, because this is a new problem
options.why: setIfAbsent already returned true for one caller. Later runs see the flag and do not page.

options.text: It parks on a Temporal timer, holds no VM, and re-checks whether main is still red when the flag is cleared
options.why: A parked run costs nothing. After Resume, most such runs find main green and end as not_needed.

check.q: be-ci-fixer's last 5 finished runs ended merged, failed, handed_off, rejected and failed. Does the circuit breaker trip?

options.text: Yes: failed, rejected and failed are 3 bad runs out of 5
options.why: Only failed and rejected count, and there are three of them. handed_off and merged do not count.

options.text: No, because one of its runs was merged
options.why: One good run does not cancel three bad ones. The rule only counts the bad outcomes.

options.text: No, because handed_off means the breaker must wait for the environment
options.why: handed_off is simply not counted. The other three bad outcomes are still enough to trip.

p: storm.ts lives in orchestrator/src/activities/ next to stillRed. The CI and pipeline-fixer charters set gather_minutes: 7, so routineRun sleeps before its gate while addTrigger signals pile up. stormCheck counts with client.workflow.count on the Routine and RunKind search attributes that routineRun registers on the ai-agents namespace. Above 5 in 15 minutes it sets routines:fixers:paused in the G3 kill-switch flag store, pages through a PagerDuty service for ai-agents that DevOps creates, and posts the fingerprints to #ai-agents-alerts with a Resume fixers button. preRunGate parks cifix runs while the flag is set.

circuitBreaker is in the same file and runs as the last step of every routineRun. routineRun sets RoutineOutcome when it ends (merged, closed, rejected, failed, handed_off, not_needed). A trip sets routine:<name>:paused, messages the owner with the 5 runs, and shows up in the next team digest. The storm test is a replay in a test namespace: 8 saved red-build events in 2 minutes must give one page and zero VMs.

tickets.why: The gather window, stillRed, stormCheck, incident mode and the one page.
RoutineOutcome and the circuit breaker: 3 failed or rejected of the last 5 pause the routine.

words.plain: A flag that parks every new fixer run and pages one person, set when more than 5 new fingerprints arrive in 15 minutes.
A question to Temporal's searchable list of runs, in a small SQL-like language, for example counting runs started after a time.
An indexed field set on a run, such as Routine or RunKind, that visibility queries can filter on.
Set a flag only if nobody has set it yet, and report whether this call was the one that set it.
A rule that pauses one routine when 3 of its last 5 finished runs failed or were rejected, until its owner resumes it.

review.q: From memory: the storm rule (how many, in what window) and the three things incident mode does.
review.a: More than 5 new fingerprints in 15 minutes. It sets routines:fixers:paused, pages the on-call person once, and posts the first errors to #ai-agents-alerts with a Resume button; new fixer runs then park at the gate.

review.q: After the incident is cleared, what happens to the parked runs, and why does the 10:02 broken-test run still get fixed?
review.a: Each re-checks that main is still red at its latest commit. The install failures are green after the runner fix, so those end as not_needed. The broken test is a real code problem, still red, so its run goes on to a VM.

review.q: Which run outcomes count against a routine in the circuit breaker, and why not the others?
review.a: Only failed and rejected. handed_off is usually the environment and not_needed means main healed itself; neither is the routine's fault.

remember: Count causes, not builds: many new fingerprints at once means the environment, so park every fixer and page one person once; a routine that keeps failing pauses itself.
